cases.case_title: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru and Others v. State of Kerala and Another
cases.paragraph_anchors: Paras 284-292 (Sikri C.J.), Paras 646-652 (Shelat & Grover JJ.), Paras 1184-1212 (Khanna J.)
cases.holding_summary: Parliament has wide power under Article 368 to amend any provision of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, but this power does not extend to altering or destroying the 'Basic Structure' or essential framework of the Constitution. The unreviewable conclusive declaration clause of Article 31C struck down as violative of judicial review.

doctrinal_relationships.rationale: Amending power constrained by Basic Structure doctrine
Second part of Article 31C barring judicial review struck down
Overruled Golak Nath's proposition that constitutional amendments are ordinary law under Art 13(2)

cases.case_title: Minerva Mills Ltd. and Others v. Union of India and Others
cases.outcome_breakdown: 4:1 Majority (Bhagwati J. concurring in part, dissenting in part)
cases.holding_summary: Sections 4 and 55 of the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976 held unconstitutional. Clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 seeking to exclude judicial review and confer unlimited amending power violated the basic structure. The harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles (Part IV) is an essential feature of the Constitution.

doctrinal_relationships.rationale: Exclusion of judicial review from amendments is unconstitutional
Conferment of absolute unlimited amending power violates basic structure
Subordination of Articles 14 and 19 to all Directive Principles struck down

cases.case_title: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India and Another
cases.holding_summary: The 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 cannot be arbitrary, fanciful, or oppressive; it must be just, fair, and reasonable, incorporating the principles of natural justice. The Golden Triangle doctrine established that Articles 14, 19, and 21 are not mutually exclusive water-tight compartments but form an interwoven tapestry of constitutional liberty.

doctrinal_relationships.rationale: Procedure depriving personal liberty must satisfy substantive fairness and natural justice
Overruled Gopalan's siloed compartmentalization of Fundamental Rights

cases.case_title: I.R. Coelho (Dead) by LRs v. State of Tamil Nadu and Others
cases.holding_summary: Any law inserted into the Ninth Schedule by constitutional amendment on or after 24 April 1973 (the date of Kesavananda Bharati) does not enjoy blanket immunity from judicial review. If such a law violates the Fundamental Rights guaranteed under Articles 14, 19, or 21 and the violation touches the Basic Structure, it will be struck down.

doctrinal_relationships.rationale: Blanket immunity curtailed post-24.04.1973; subject to basic structure review
Judicial review is an unalterable basic feature

cases.case_title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) and Another v. Union of India and Others
cases.outcome_breakdown: Unanimous 9:0 on core holding (6 concurring opinions)
cases.holding_summary: The right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution. Explicitly overruled M.P. Sharma (1954 - 8 judges) and ADM Jabalpur (1976 - 5 judges) to the extent they held privacy not protected. Enacted a 3-fold proportionality test for state infringement (legality, legitimate aim, proportionality).

doctrinal_relationships.rationale: Privacy recognized as fundamental right intrinsic to human dignity
Overruled to the extent it denied constitutional right to privacy
Formally overruled majority view on suspension of Art. 21 during Emergency

cases.case_title: S.R. Bommai and Others v. Union of India and Others
cases.outcome_breakdown: 9-judge bench (plurality / majority by Sawant, Kuldip Singh, Jeevan Reddy JJ.)
cases.holding_summary: A Presidential proclamation under Article 356 imposing President's Rule in a State is not immune from judicial review; it can be struck down if issued mala fide or on extraneous or irrelevant grounds. Secularism and federalism are basic features of the Constitution. The floor of the Legislative Assembly is the sole constitutional venue for testing the majority of a Ministry.

doctrinal_relationships.rationale: Subjected to judicial review; assembly cannot be dissolved until Parliament approves
Bar on inquiring into ministerial advice does not bar court from inspecting underlying material

cases.case_title: In re: The Delhi Laws Act, 1912, the Ajmer-Merwara (Extension of Laws) Act, 1947 and the Part C States (Laws) Act, 1950
cases.paragraph_anchors: 1951 SCR 747 at 787 (Fazl Ali J.), at 846 (Mukherjea J.)
cases.holding_summary: Foundational constitutional doctrine on limits of delegated legislation in India. The Legislature cannot abdicate its 'essential legislative function'—which consists of determining legislative policy and formulating it into a binding rule of conduct. Subordinate, ancillary, or conditional delegation is constitutionally valid, but empowering the executive to repeal or modify existing legislative policies is ultra vires.

doctrinal_relationships.rationale: Legislative power includes power to delegate non-essential functions
Essential legislative function cannot be delegated to the executive

cases.case_title: The State of Madras v. Srimathi Champakam Dorairajan and Another
cases.outcome_breakdown: Unanimous 7:0 (Judgment delivered by S.R. Das, J.)
cases.holding_summary: Communal G.O. of the Madras Government allocating seats in medical and engineering colleges on the basis of religion and caste was struck down as violating Article 29(2). Held that Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV, including Art. 46) cannot override Fundamental Rights (Part III). Prompted Parliament to enact the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951 inserting Article 15(4).

doctrinal_relationships.rationale: State-maintained educational admissions cannot discriminate on ground of religion, race, or caste
Directive principles must conform and remain subsidiary to Fundamental Rights
Directly led to enactment of Article 15(4) via First Amendment
